items.item: Every structure earlier in this chapter answered a location question (where does this key live); this topic asks an agreement question instead (do these two copies match) and says so explicitly as the chapter's turn.

at.step: Consistent hashing answers where a piece of data lives. It says nothing about whether two copies of it actually agree. This topic proves they do, without comparing either one whole.

items.item: A Merkle tree's root hash is built by recursively hashing pairs of child hashes, not by hashing the whole dataset in one pass — the recursive structure is what makes the O(log n) walk-down possible.

at.step: Hash each piece of data, then hash the hashes, two at a time, all the way up. One number at the top speaks for everything underneath it.

items.item: A matching root hash is not merely probabilistic reassurance — with a cryptographic hash, it is as strong a guarantee as comparing every leaf, because any leaf difference provably propagates to the root.

at.step: Two trees, two root hashes — they match. What does that actually tell you?

items.item: A root mismatch alone proves disagreement exists, without yet saying where — the two facts (disagreement exists; disagreement's location) are answered by two different operations at two different costs.

at.step: A mismatched root tells you the two copies disagree somewhere — but not yet where.

items.item: Finding one changed leaf costs about log n hash comparisons by walking from the root, following only the one child whose hash disagrees at each level — not n, and not a random search.

at.step: One leaf out of many changed. How many hashes do you have to check to find which one?

items.item: The walk-down's correctness depends on exactly the same argument as the authentication direction: only one branch beneath a disagreement can be the source, so the other branch is provably safe to skip.

at.step: At each level, only one child can be wrong. Follow that branch down, and you reach the exact leaf in about log n steps.

items.item: Anti-entropy repair, Git's object model, and certificate transparency are three independent real systems built on the same Merkle-tree mechanism, each verified against its own current primary source rather than assumed from the structure's theoretical description.

items.item: Fixed-offset chunking's weakness isn't the chunking itself — it's that a length-changing edit shifts the byte position of everything after it, and therefore every later boundary and every later chunk's hash.

at.step: Split data into fixed-size pieces, and one early edit shifts every boundary after it. Split it where the data's own content says to, and only one boundary moves.

items.item: Content-defined chunking fixes this by making boundaries a function of nearby content rather than a running byte count, so an edit's effect on chunk boundaries stays local to where the edit happened.
This topic's own measured numbers (hashes checked, chunks reshaped) come from a from-scratch tree and stream built in examples.py, not from any cited system's own benchmarked performance.
